content: {"id": "219450e7-f185-4e76-bf25-1eb41f49a5f8", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Hypothetical for the DynamoDB latency skill \u2014 no AWS calls. Table catalog-test, 3-hour window. Query shows SystemErrors of 240 across 12 consecutive periods 13:00\u201313:11, and FaultInjectionServiceInducedErrors for Query is exactly 240 in the same periods. Query p99 rose to 130 ms against its 7-day baseline of 30 ms in those periods, with thousands of requests per period; p50 stayed at baseline. Our SystemErrors alarm fired. Is DynamoDB having a service problem?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "37625547-5593-4bf9-8482-e6d8c4622517", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "No — this looks like a self-inflicted condition, not a DynamoDB service-side problem.

The key signal is that `FaultInjectionServiceInducedErrors` for Query is exactly 240 in the same 12 periods as `SystemErrors` (240). When fault-injection-induced errors account for the entirety of the `SystemErrors` count, those "errors" are from the **Fault Injection Simulator (FIS)** deliberately injecting server-side errors against the table (or a chaos-engineering/resilience test using that same mechanism) — not an actual DynamoDB outage or degradation. DynamoDB's own health is not implicated; the errors are synthetic and expected under a fault-injection test.

That also explains the rest of the pattern cleanly:
- **p99 rose to 130 ms vs. a 30 ms baseline, while p50 stayed flat at baseline.** Fault injection on a sampled subset of requests drags the tail (retries/errors push some requests' effective latency up) without touching the bulk of traffic — classic "tail elevation driven by injected faults," not a broad latency regression.
- **Thousands of requests per period** with only 240 affected per period is consistent with a bounded, intentional injection rate rather than an uncontrolled service issue.
- **The SystemErrors alarm firing** is expected — the alarm doesn't distinguish "real" SystemErrors from fault-injected ones, so it will trip during an active FIS experiment even though DynamoDB itself is healthy.

Net: this maps to the skill's "fault-injection/test-induced" explanation rather than "service-side errors" or genuine "tail elevation." The practical move is to correlate the 13:00–13:11 window with any active FIS experiment template/run against catalog-test — if one was running, this is the test working as intended, and the alarm is a false positive for real customer impact (though you may still want it to page so someone confirms the experiment is bounded and rolled back on schedule).

If you want, I can walk through how this would differ if the FaultInjectionServiceInducedErrors count were only a fraction of total SystemErrors instead of matching it exactly.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
